[[File:板石積石棺墓（地下式板石積石室墓）.png|350px|thumb|{{ill|Schematic diagram of an Underground stone slab tomb|ja|板石積石棺墓（地下式板石積石室墓）|lt=Schematic diagram of an Underground stone slab tomb|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Schematic diagram of an Underground stone slab tomb|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}]]
'''stone slab tomb''' (板石積石棺墓), also known as '''Underground stone slab tomb''' (地下式板石積石室墓), is a type of Sarcophagus tomb in which a circular or square burial pit is excavated in the ground and flat stone slabs are arranged vertically along the walls, being successively overlapped in a “carrying” manner to form a lid. It is recognized as a regionally distinctive tomb style that emerged during the 4th–5th centuries of the {{ill|Kofun period|en|Kofun period|WD=Q459939|lt=Kofun period}} in the southern part of the {{ill|Kyushu region|ja|九州地方|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kyushu region|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 九州|1=Kyushu|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q13987}}, particularly from the northwestern part of {{ill|Kagoshima Prefecture|en|Kagoshima Prefecture|WD=Q15701|lt=Kagoshima Prefecture}}, extending to the island areas along the western coast of Kyushu and the southwestern part of {{ill|Miyazaki Prefecture|en|Miyazaki Prefecture|WD=Q130300|lt=Miyazaki Prefecture}}.

==Overview==

=== structure ===
A burial pit of either circular or square plan is excavated in the ground. Along its walls, stone slabs (known as side stones) are set upright so as to form a Sarcophagus (the burial facility). Flat stone slabs are then laid on top of the side stones and further slabs are gradually overlapped with slight offsets—a method known as “carrying”—to build up the height and form a domed ceiling lid. Finally, the pit is backfilled with earth, thus creating an underground burial space. When the overlying soil is removed during excavation surveys, especially in cases with a circular plan, the dome structure formed by the overlapping slabs often exhibits a characteristic “fish-scale” or “chrysanthemum” appearance. Variations exist in plan shape, with some tombs being circular and others square or rectangular, and several classification schemes have been proposed. Debates continue regarding which form predates the other, as well as the origins and genealogical development of this tomb style.

=== Group Structure ===
It is extremely rare for a single stone slab tomb to be constructed in isolation; instead, they are typically found clustered in groups of two to three or even in dense groups of more than a dozen. Accordingly, the archaeological site is usually designated as “(Place Name) + stone slab tomb Group.” However, because they often occur alongside tombs from other periods—such as earthen mound tombs or Underground Horizontal Yokoanabos—some sites are simply referred to as “(Place Name) + Site.”

=== Above-ground structures ===
In most cases, there are no surface structures or markers resembling the tumuli of keyhole-shaped Kofuns. Consequently, the locations of these tombs were often not recognized by later generations. There are instances where a sudden collapse of the burial chamber ceiling caused the ground surface to subside, leading to the tomb’s discovery, or where agricultural activities (such as plowing or land improvement) resulted in farm animals or tractors becoming caught in a collapsed chamber, effectively uncovering the tomb accidentally.<ref name="Sfn|藤井|2009"/> In recent years, buried cultural property surveys have sometimes employed ground-penetrating radar to identify the tomb locations. Furthermore, the Board of Education of Miyazaki City has issued warnings on its website regarding sudden ground subsidence in agricultural fields, noting that such events may indicate the presence of an Underground stone slab tomb.

== About the name ==
In the past, the name “Underground Taiseki Stone Chamber Tomb” (地下式板石積石室墓) was commonly used; however, because its origins lie in the construction of a “Sarcophagus” rather than a “stone chamber,” and since there is no corresponding “surface type” tomb with the same stone slab construction, the qualifier “underground” has lost its contrasting meaning. Consequently, in recent years the name “stone slab tomb” has come to be regarded as more appropriate.<ref name="Sfn|藤井|2009"/>

== Grave goods ==
Generally, few funerary goods are found in these tombs. Many contain no grave goods or only minimal iron weapons (such as swords and iron arrowheads), which has complicated the development of chronological frameworks and the establishment of a chronology for this tomb style. Among the iron weapons, iron arrowheads are most frequently recovered; these include forms such as the Keitō arrowhead, bird-beak arrowhead, and short-necked arrowhead.

== distribution ==
The distribution of stone slab tombs extends from the northern limit marked by the Ushimoku stone slab tomb Group in Ōaza Kamie, {{ill|Takanabe, Miyazaki|en|Takanabe, Miyazaki|WD=Q1206737|lt=Takanabe Town}}, {{ill|Koyu District, Miyazaki|en|Koyu District, Miyazaki|WD=Q1132169|lt=Koyugu District}}, {{ill|Miyazaki Prefecture|en|Miyazaki Prefecture|WD=Q130300|lt=Miyazaki Prefecture}}, to the southern limit represented by the Nakao stone slab tomb Group in {{ill|Aira, Kagoshima (Kimotsuki District)|en|Aira, Kagoshima (Kimotsuki District)|WD=Q4698402|lt=Awa-cho}}, {{ill|Kanoya, Kagoshima|en|Kanoya, Kagoshima|WD=Q819578|lt=Kanoya City}}, {{ill|Kagoshima Prefecture|en|Kagoshima Prefecture|WD=Q15701|lt=Kagoshima Prefecture}}. They are mainly distributed throughout the Miyazaki Plain, extending into basins in areas such as {{ill|Miyakonojō|en|Miyakonojō|WD=Q638301|lt=Tosu City}}, {{ill|Kobayashi, Miyazaki|en|Kobayashi, Miyazaki|WD=Q861283|lt=Kobayashi City}}, and {{ill|Ebino, Miyazaki|en|Ebino, Miyazaki|WD=Q374701|lt=Ebino City}} at the northern foothills of the {{ill|Kirishima Volcanic Group|ja|霧島火山群|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kirishima Volcanic Group|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 霧島山|1=Mount Kirishima|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q1319361}}, with the western boundary defined by the Harumura stone slab tomb Group in {{ill|Isa, Kagoshima|en|Isa, Kagoshima|WD=Q15736|lt=Isa City}}, {{ill|Kagoshima Prefecture|en|Kagoshima Prefecture|WD=Q15701|lt=Kagoshima Prefecture}}. Additionally, two tombs have been identified at the Tendōgao site in {{ill|Hitoyoshi, Kumamoto|en|Hitoyoshi, Kumamoto|WD=Q861292|lt=Hitoyoshi City}}, {{ill|Kumamoto Prefecture|en|Kumamoto Prefecture|WD=Q130308|lt=Kumamoto Prefecture}}, indicating that the northwestern extent of this tomb style reaches into the basin of the {{ill|Kuma River (Japan)|en|Kuma River (Japan)|WD=Q1358183|lt=Kumagawa River}}.

== Roots and development ==
The initial form of this tomb style is thought to be the “Yokuguchi-style Earthen Tomb” that appeared from the latter half of the early Kofun period to the early mid-Kofun period, discovered within a subgroup of the {{ill|Kogihara Underground Horizontal Yokoanabo Group|ja|小木原地下式横穴墓群|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kogihara Underground Horizontal Yokoanabo Group|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} in {{ill|Kobayashi, Miyazaki|en|Kobayashi, Miyazaki|WD=Q861283|lt=Kobayashi City}}, {{ill|Miyazaki Prefecture|en|Miyazaki Prefecture|WD=Q130300|lt=Miyazaki Prefecture}}. Subsequently, based on the shape of the burial chamber, these tombs were broadly categorized into two types—the “houseform type” and the “earthen mound type”—which spread regionally from the 5th to the 6th centuries.<ref name="Sfn|橋本|2012|p=143"/>

== Research History ==
Records of Underground Horizontal Yokoanabos date back to the {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period}} and even earlier to the {{ill|Meiji period|ja|明治期|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Meiji period|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 明治|1=Meiji period|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q3125096}}. In the work ''{{ill|Keirin Manroku|ja|桂林漫録|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Keirin Manroku|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}'' by {{ill|Mori Island Nakayoshi|ja|森島（桂川）中良|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mori Island Nakayoshi|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, the younger brother of {{ill|Katsuragawa Hoshū|en|Katsuragawa Hoshū|WD=Q946932|lt=Katsuragawa Hoshu}}, an account from 1789 (the 1st year of {{ill|Kansei|en|Kansei|WD=Q1195131|lt=Kansei}}) describes a farmer in {{ill|Hyūga Province|en|Hyūga Province|WD=Q513737|lt=Hyūga Province}} near the pig mound at {{ill|Inoh-tsuka|ja|猪の塚|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Inoh-tsuka|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} (located in {{ill|Miyazaki Prefecture|en|Miyazaki Prefecture|WD=Q130300|lt=Miyazaki Prefecture}}, {{ill|Higashimorokata District, Miyazaki|en|Higashimorokata District, Miyazaki|WD=Q1132180|lt=Higashimorokata District}}, {{ill|Kunitomi, Miyazaki|en|Kunitomi, Miyazaki|WD=Q1350786|lt=Kunimoto Town}}, Honjō) who, while digging a trench, encountered a horizontal cave with its walls painted in vermilion, from which numerous relics were unearthed. Local historian {{ill|Senokuchi Denkurō|ja|瀬之口伝九郎|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Senokuchi Denkurō|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} regarded this as the earliest literary reference to an Underground Horizontal Yokoanabo.<ref name="Sfn|瀬之口|1919"/> In modern times, archaeological research began in earnest, and Senokuchi Denkurō coined the term “Underground-type Tomb” to classify it as one form of Kofun period burial system.<ref name="Sfn|瀬之口|1919"/>

Subsequently, studies employing archaeological methods—such as the classification of plan and cross-sectional morphologies, chronological analyses based on grave good assemblages, and examinations of the relationship between these tombs and keyhole-shaped tumuli—have steadily advanced.<ref name="Sfn|日高|1958"/><ref name="Sfn|石川|1973"/>

=== Discussion on "Hayato Burial System" ===
Parallel to these developments, a theory emerged proposing that Underground Horizontal Yokoanabos, owing to their unique structure, concentrated distribution in southern Kyushu, and the extremely sparse presence of keyhole-shaped tumuli in their principal distribution areas, were the tombs of the “Hayato,” a group regarded in ancient texts as peripheral by the centralized {{ill|Ritsuryō state|ja|律令国家|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ritsuryō state|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 律令制|1=ritsuryō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q742460}}.<ref name="Sfn|高橋|1924"/> During the 1960s–80s, as comprehensive views of the Kofun period were synthesized, several scholars posited that stone slab tombs corresponded to the “Hayato tomb system” of the Hyūga–Ōsumi region, that Underground stone slab tombs in Satsuma corresponded to the “Satsuma Hayato tomb system,” and that certain tumuli-associated tombs in the southern Satsuma Peninsula represented the “Ata Hayato tomb system.”<ref name="Sfn|小田|1966|p=163"/><ref name="Sfn|乙益|1970"/><ref name="Sfn|上村|1984"/> Their formation was attributed to the region’s volcanic soils, limited flatlands unsuitable for rice cultivation, and its isolation from external influences, which led to a stagnation in cultural change from the Yayoi period onward and the establishment of an independent local sphere. This conceptualization—portraying the “specialized underground tomb system in southern Kyushu” as “Hayato tombs” in contrast to the expansive dominion of the {{ill|Yamato court|ja|大和朝廷|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yamato court|ja_comment=|2=ja|3=ヤマト王権|1=Yamato Kinship|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q2658252}}—gained widespread acceptance.

However, by the 1990s, many researchers, particularly local scholars in Kyushu, began to question the appropriateness of linking Underground Horizontal Yokoanabos with the “Hayato.”

The term “Hayato” first appears in the mythological portions of the {{ill|Kojiki|en|Kojiki|WD=Q813031|lt=Kojiki}}, and while it is mentioned from the time of Emperor Nintoku, its use as a confirmed historical term is generally recognized only from the 11th month of the 11th year of the {{ill|Tenmu period|ja|天武朝|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tenmu period|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} (682 AD, in records of Hayato tributary missions).<ref name="Sfn|中村|1993"/> Furthermore, the peak of Underground Horizontal Yokoanabo construction occurred during the 5th to 6th centuries, and there are no definitively dated examples persisting into the latter Kofun period (6th century). Similarly, Underground Horizontal Yokoanabos considered to be “Hayato tombs” in the Hyūga–Ōsumi region were primarily built in the 5th to 6th centuries, ceasing by the early 7th century. As for the so-called “Ata Hayato tombs” (represented by Tateishi Doikombō), the securely dated examples date from the mid-Yayoi to the early Kofun period, and in that region (from the southern tip of the Satsuma Peninsula to the coastal areas of Kagoshima Bay), tomb types without tumuli or with pottery coffins are predominant, making it less tenable to designate that tomb system solely as “Ata Hayato tombs.” Moreover, some scholars argue that the very concept of “Hayato” was a pseudo-ethnic construct, politically created by the Ritsuryō government based on Sinocentric ideology, rather than arising from indigenous ethnic differences.<ref name="Sfn|永山|2009|pp=40"/><ref name="Sfn|中村|1993"/><ref name="Sfn|東|2001|p=498"/><ref name="Sfn|原口|2008"/><ref name="Sfn|原口|2011"/>

=== Research after the theory of "Hayato Burial System" ===
From the 2000s onward, research on stone slab tombs has increasingly employed extensive excavation data and artifact assemblages to examine these tombs using rigorous archaeological methods, conceptualizing them as a regional burial system of the Kofun period. Detailed studies now focus on classification based on structural morphology, chronological frameworks derived from grave good composition and distribution patterns, and reconstructions of social hierarchy and regional structure based on the relationship with keyhole-shaped tumuli.<ref name="Sfn|第6回九州前方後円墳研究会|2003"/><ref name="Sfn|橋本|2009c"/><ref name="Sfn|藤井|2009"/>

[[File:板石積石棺墓（地下式板石積石室墓）.png|350px|thumb|{{ill|Schematic diagram of an Underground stone slab tomb|ja|板石積石棺墓（地下式板石積石室墓）|lt=Schematic diagram of an Underground stone slab tomb|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Schematic diagram of an Underground stone slab tomb|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}]]
'''stone slab tomb''' (板石積石棺墓), also known as '''Underground stone slab tomb''' (地下式板石積石室墓), is a type of Sarcophagus tomb in which a circular or square burial pit is excavated in the ground and flat stone slabs are arranged vertically along the walls, being successively overlapped in a “carrying” manner to form a lid. It is recognized as a regionally distinctive tomb style that emerged during the 4th–5th centuries of the {{ill|Kofun period|en|Kofun period|WD=Q459939|lt=Kofun period|1=Kofun period}} in the southern part of the {{ill|Kyushu region|ja|九州地方|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kyushu region|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 九州|1=Kyushu|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q13987}}, particularly from the northwestern part of {{ill|Kagoshima Prefecture|en|Kagoshima Prefecture|WD=Q15701|lt=Kagoshima Prefecture|1=Kagoshima Prefecture}}, extending to the island areas along the western coast of Kyushu and the southwestern part of {{ill|Miyazaki Prefecture|en|Miyazaki Prefecture|WD=Q130300|lt=Miyazaki Prefecture|1=Miyazaki Prefecture}}.

==Overview==

=== structure ===
A burial pit of either circular or square plan is excavated in the ground. Along its walls, stone slabs (known as side stones) are set upright so as to form a Sarcophagus (the burial facility). Flat stone slabs are then laid on top of the side stones and further slabs are gradually overlapped with slight offsets—a method known as “carrying”—to build up the height and form a domed ceiling lid. Finally, the pit is backfilled with earth, thus creating an underground burial space. When the overlying soil is removed during excavation surveys, especially in cases with a circular plan, the dome structure formed by the overlapping slabs often exhibits a characteristic “fish-scale” or “chrysanthemum” appearance. Variations exist in plan shape, with some tombs being circular and others square or rectangular, and several classification schemes have been proposed. Debates continue regarding which form predates the other, as well as the origins and genealogical development of this tomb style.

=== Group Structure ===
It is extremely rare for a single stone slab tomb to be constructed in isolation; instead, they are typically found clustered in groups of two to three or even in dense groups of more than a dozen. Accordingly, the archaeological site is usually designated as “(Place Name) + stone slab tomb Group.” However, because they often occur alongside tombs from other periods—such as earthen mound tombs or Underground Horizontal Yokoanabos—some sites are simply referred to as “(Place Name) + Site.”

=== Above-ground structures ===
In most cases, there are no surface structures or markers resembling the tumuli of keyhole-shaped Kofuns. Consequently, the locations of these tombs were often not recognized by later generations. There are instances where a sudden collapse of the burial chamber ceiling caused the ground surface to subside, leading to the tomb’s discovery, or where agricultural activities (such as plowing or land improvement) resulted in farm animals or tractors becoming caught in a collapsed chamber, effectively uncovering the tomb accidentally.<ref name="Sfn|藤井|2009"/> In recent years, buried cultural property surveys have sometimes employed ground-penetrating radar to identify the tomb locations. Furthermore, the Board of Education of Miyazaki City has issued warnings on its website regarding sudden ground subsidence in agricultural fields, noting that such events may indicate the presence of an Underground stone slab tomb.

== About the name ==
In the past, the name “Underground Taiseki Stone Chamber Tomb” (地下式板石積石室墓) was commonly used; however, because its origins lie in the construction of a “Sarcophagus” rather than a “stone chamber,” and since there is no corresponding “surface type” tomb with the same stone slab construction, the qualifier “underground” has lost its contrasting meaning. Consequently, in recent years the name “stone slab tomb” has come to be regarded as more appropriate.<ref name="Sfn|藤井|2009"/>

== Grave goods ==
Generally, few funerary goods are found in these tombs. Many contain no grave goods or only minimal iron weapons (such as swords and iron arrowheads), which has complicated the development of chronological frameworks and the establishment of a chronology for this tomb style. Among the iron weapons, iron arrowheads are most frequently recovered; these include forms such as the Keitō arrowhead, bird-beak arrowhead, and short-necked arrowhead.

== distribution ==
The distribution of stone slab tombs extends from the northern limit marked by the Ushimoku stone slab tomb Group in Ōaza Kamie, {{ill|Takanabe, Miyazaki|en|Takanabe, Miyazaki|WD=Q1206737|lt=Takanabe Town|1=Takanabe, Miyazaki}}, {{ill|Koyu District, Miyazaki|en|Koyu District, Miyazaki|WD=Q1132169|lt=Koyugu District|1=Koyu District, Miyazaki}}, {{ill|Miyazaki Prefecture|en|Miyazaki Prefecture|WD=Q130300|lt=Miyazaki Prefecture|1=Miyazaki Prefecture}}, to the southern limit represented by the Nakao stone slab tomb Group in {{ill|Aira, Kagoshima (Kimotsuki District)|en|Aira, Kagoshima (Kimotsuki District)|WD=Q4698402|lt=Awa-cho|1=Aira, Kagoshima (Kimotsuki District)}}, {{ill|Kanoya, Kagoshima|en|Kanoya, Kagoshima|WD=Q819578|lt=Kanoya City|1=Kanoya, Kagoshima}}, {{ill|Kagoshima Prefecture|en|Kagoshima Prefecture|WD=Q15701|lt=Kagoshima Prefecture|1=Kagoshima Prefecture}}. They are mainly distributed throughout the Miyazaki Plain, extending into basins in areas such as {{ill|Miyakonojō|en|Miyakonojō|WD=Q638301|lt=Tosu City|1=Miyakonojō}}, {{ill|Kobayashi, Miyazaki|en|Kobayashi, Miyazaki|WD=Q861283|lt=Kobayashi City|1=Kobayashi, Miyazaki}}, and {{ill|Ebino, Miyazaki|en|Ebino, Miyazaki|WD=Q374701|lt=Ebino City|1=Ebino, Miyazaki}} at the northern foothills of the {{ill|Kirishima Volcanic Group|ja|霧島火山群|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kirishima Volcanic Group|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 霧島山|1=Mount Kirishima|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q1319361}}, with the western boundary defined by the Harumura stone slab tomb Group in {{ill|Isa, Kagoshima|en|Isa, Kagoshima|WD=Q15736|lt=Isa City|1=Isa, Kagoshima}}, {{ill|Kagoshima Prefecture|en|Kagoshima Prefecture|WD=Q15701|lt=Kagoshima Prefecture|1=Kagoshima Prefecture}}. Additionally, two tombs have been identified at the Tendōgao site in {{ill|Hitoyoshi, Kumamoto|en|Hitoyoshi, Kumamoto|WD=Q861292|lt=Hitoyoshi City|1=Hitoyoshi, Kumamoto}}, {{ill|Kumamoto Prefecture|en|Kumamoto Prefecture|WD=Q130308|lt=Kumamoto Prefecture|1=Kumamoto Prefecture}}, indicating that the northwestern extent of this tomb style reaches into the basin of the {{ill|Kuma River (Japan)|en|Kuma River (Japan)|WD=Q1358183|lt=Kumagawa River|1=Kuma River (Japan)}}.

== Roots and development ==
The initial form of this tomb style is thought to be the “Yokuguchi-style Earthen Tomb” that appeared from the latter half of the early Kofun period to the early mid-Kofun period, discovered within a subgroup of the {{ill|Kogihara Underground Horizontal Yokoanabo Group|ja|小木原地下式横穴墓群|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kogihara Underground Horizontal Yokoanabo Group|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} in {{ill|Kobayashi, Miyazaki|en|Kobayashi, Miyazaki|WD=Q861283|lt=Kobayashi City|1=Kobayashi, Miyazaki}}, {{ill|Miyazaki Prefecture|en|Miyazaki Prefecture|WD=Q130300|lt=Miyazaki Prefecture|1=Miyazaki Prefecture}}. Subsequently, based on the shape of the burial chamber, these tombs were broadly categorized into two types—the “houseform type” and the “earthen mound type”—which spread regionally from the 5th to the 6th centuries.<ref name="Sfn|橋本|2012|p=143"/>

== Research History ==
Records of Underground Horizontal Yokoanabos date back to the {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period|1=Edo period}} and even earlier to the {{ill|Meiji period|ja|明治期|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Meiji period|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 明治|1=Meiji era|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q3125096}}. In the work ''{{ill|Keirin Manroku|ja|桂林漫録|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Keirin Manroku|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}'' by {{ill|Mori Island Nakayoshi|ja|森島（桂川）中良|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mori Island Nakayoshi|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, the younger brother of {{ill|Katsuragawa Hoshū|en|Katsuragawa Hoshū|WD=Q946932|lt=Katsuragawa Hoshu|1=Katsuragawa Hoshū}}, an account from 1789 (the 1st year of {{ill|Kansei|en|Kansei|WD=Q1195131|lt=Kansei|1=Kansei}}) describes a farmer in {{ill|Hyūga Province|en|Hyūga Province|WD=Q513737|lt=Hyūga Province|1=Hyūga Province}} near the pig mound at {{ill|Inoh-tsuka|ja|猪の塚|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Inoh-tsuka|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} (located in {{ill|Miyazaki Prefecture|en|Miyazaki Prefecture|WD=Q130300|lt=Miyazaki Prefecture|1=Miyazaki Prefecture}}, {{ill|Higashimorokata District, Miyazaki|en|Higashimorokata District, Miyazaki|WD=Q1132180|lt=Higashimorokata District|1=Higashimorokata District, Miyazaki}}, {{ill|Kunitomi, Miyazaki|en|Kunitomi, Miyazaki|WD=Q1350786|lt=Kunimoto Town|1=Kunitomi, Miyazaki}}, Honjō) who, while digging a trench, encountered a horizontal cave with its walls painted in vermilion, from which numerous relics were unearthed. Local historian {{ill|Senokuchi Denkurō|ja|瀬之口伝九郎|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Senokuchi Denkurō|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} regarded this as the earliest literary reference to an Underground Horizontal Yokoanabo.<ref name="Sfn|瀬之口|1919"/> In modern times, archaeological research began in earnest, and Senokuchi Denkurō coined the term “Underground-type Tomb” to classify it as one form of Kofun period burial system.<ref name="Sfn|瀬之口|1919"/>

Subsequently, studies employing archaeological methods—such as the classification of plan and cross-sectional morphologies, chronological analyses based on grave good assemblages, and examinations of the relationship between these tombs and keyhole-shaped tumuli—have steadily advanced.<ref name="Sfn|日高|1958"/><ref name="Sfn|石川|1973"/>

=== Discussion on "Hayato Burial System" ===
Parallel to these developments, a theory emerged proposing that Underground Horizontal Yokoanabos, owing to their unique structure, concentrated distribution in southern Kyushu, and the extremely sparse presence of keyhole-shaped tumuli in their principal distribution areas, were the tombs of the “Hayato,” a group regarded in ancient texts as peripheral by the centralized {{ill|Ritsuryō state|ja|律令国家|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ritsuryō state|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 律令制|1=Ritsuryō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q742460}}.<ref name="Sfn|高橋|1924"/> During the 1960s–80s, as comprehensive views of the Kofun period were synthesized, several scholars posited that stone slab tombs corresponded to the “Hayato tomb system” of the Hyūga–Ōsumi region, that Underground stone slab tombs in Satsuma corresponded to the “Satsuma Hayato tomb system,” and that certain tumuli-associated tombs in the southern Satsuma Peninsula represented the “Ata Hayato tomb system.”<ref name="Sfn|小田|1966|p=163"/><ref name="Sfn|乙益|1970"/><ref name="Sfn|上村|1984"/> Their formation was attributed to the region’s volcanic soils, limited flatlands unsuitable for rice cultivation, and its isolation from external influences, which led to a stagnation in cultural change from the Yayoi period onward and the establishment of an independent local sphere. This conceptualization—portraying the “specialized underground tomb system in southern Kyushu” as “Hayato tombs” in contrast to the expansive dominion of the {{ill|Yamato court|ja|大和朝廷|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yamato court|ja_comment=|2=ja|3=ヤマト王権|1=Yamato Kingship|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q2658252}}—gained widespread acceptance.

However, by the 1990s, many researchers, particularly local scholars in Kyushu, began to question the appropriateness of linking Underground Horizontal Yokoanabos with the “Hayato.”

The term “Hayato” first appears in the mythological portions of the {{ill|Kojiki|en|Kojiki|WD=Q813031|lt=Kojiki|1=Kojiki}}, and while it is mentioned from the time of Emperor Nintoku, its use as a confirmed historical term is generally recognized only from the 11th month of the 11th year of the {{ill|Tenmu period|ja|天武朝|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tenmu period|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} (682 AD, in records of Hayato tributary missions).<ref name="Sfn|中村|1993"/> Furthermore, the peak of Underground Horizontal Yokoanabo construction occurred during the 5th to 6th centuries, and there are no definitively dated examples persisting into the latter Kofun period (6th century). Similarly, Underground Horizontal Yokoanabos considered to be “Hayato tombs” in the Hyūga–Ōsumi region were primarily built in the 5th to 6th centuries, ceasing by the early 7th century. As for the so-called “Ata Hayato tombs” (represented by Tateishi Doikombō), the securely dated examples date from the mid-Yayoi to the early Kofun period, and in that region (from the southern tip of the Satsuma Peninsula to the coastal areas of Kagoshima Bay), tomb types without tumuli or with pottery coffins are predominant, making it less tenable to designate that tomb system solely as “Ata Hayato tombs.” Moreover, some scholars argue that the very concept of “Hayato” was a pseudo-ethnic construct, politically created by the Ritsuryō government based on Sinocentric ideology, rather than arising from indigenous ethnic differences.<ref name="Sfn|永山|2009|pp=40"/><ref name="Sfn|中村|1993"/><ref name="Sfn|東|2001|p=498"/><ref name="Sfn|原口|2008"/><ref name="Sfn|原口|2011"/>

=== Research after the theory of "Hayato Burial System" ===
From the 2000s onward, research on stone slab tombs has increasingly employed extensive excavation data and artifact assemblages to examine these tombs using rigorous archaeological methods, conceptualizing them as a regional burial system of the Kofun period. Detailed studies now focus on classification based on structural morphology, chronological frameworks derived from grave good composition and distribution patterns, and reconstructions of social hierarchy and regional structure based on the relationship with keyhole-shaped tumuli.<ref name="Sfn|第6回九州前方後円墳研究会|2003"/><ref name="Sfn|橋本|2009c"/><ref name="Sfn|藤井|2009"/>

[[File:板石積石棺墓（地下式板石積石室墓）.png|350px|thumb|{{ill|Schematic diagram of an Underground stone slab tomb|ja|板石積石棺墓（地下式板石積石室墓）|lt=Schematic diagram of an Underground stone slab tomb|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Schematic diagram of an Underground stone slab tomb|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}]]
'''stone slab tomb''' (板石積石棺墓), also known as '''Underground stone slab tomb''' (地下式板石積石室墓), is a type of Sarcophagus tomb in which a circular or square burial pit is excavated in the ground and flat stone slabs are arranged vertically along the walls, being successively overlapped in a “carrying” manner to form a lid. It is recognized as a regionally distinctive tomb style that emerged during the 4th–5th centuries of the {{ill|Kofun period|en|Kofun period|WD=Q459939|lt=Kofun period|1=Kofun period}} in the southern part of the {{ill|Kyushu region|ja|九州地方|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kyushu region|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 九州|1=Kyushu|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q13987}}, particularly from the northwestern part of {{ill|Kagoshima Prefecture|en|Kagoshima Prefecture|WD=Q15701|lt=Kagoshima Prefecture|1=Kagoshima Prefecture}}, extending to the island areas along the western coast of Kyushu and the southwestern part of {{ill|Miyazaki Prefecture|en|Miyazaki Prefecture|WD=Q130300|lt=Miyazaki Prefecture|1=Miyazaki Prefecture}}.

==Overview==

=== structure ===
A burial pit of either circular or square plan is excavated in the ground. Along its walls, stone slabs (known as side stones) are set upright so as to form a Sarcophagus (the burial facility). Flat stone slabs are then laid on top of the side stones and further slabs are gradually overlapped with slight offsets—a method known as “carrying”—to build up the height and form a domed ceiling lid. Finally, the pit is backfilled with earth, thus creating an underground burial space. When the overlying soil is removed during excavation surveys, especially in cases with a circular plan, the dome structure formed by the overlapping slabs often exhibits a characteristic “fish-scale” or “chrysanthemum” appearance. Variations exist in plan shape, with some tombs being circular and others square or rectangular, and several classification schemes have been proposed. Debates continue regarding which form predates the other, as well as the origins and genealogical development of this tomb style.

=== Group Structure ===
It is extremely rare for a single stone slab tomb to be constructed in isolation; instead, they are typically found clustered in groups of two to three or even in dense groups of more than a dozen. Accordingly, the archaeological site is usually designated as “(Place Name) + stone slab tomb Group.” However, because they often occur alongside tombs from other periods—such as earthen mound tombs or Underground Horizontal Yokoanabos—some sites are simply referred to as “(Place Name) + Site.”

=== Above-ground structures ===
In most cases, there are no surface structures or markers resembling the tumuli of keyhole-shaped Kofuns. Consequently, the locations of these tombs were often not recognized by later generations. There are instances where a sudden collapse of the burial chamber ceiling caused the ground surface to subside, leading to the tomb’s discovery, or where agricultural activities (such as plowing or land improvement) resulted in farm animals or tractors becoming caught in a collapsed chamber, effectively uncovering the tomb accidentally.<ref name="Sfn|藤井|2009"/> In recent years, buried cultural property surveys have sometimes employed ground-penetrating radar to identify the tomb locations. Furthermore, the Board of Education of Miyazaki City has issued warnings on its website regarding sudden ground subsidence in agricultural fields, noting that such events may indicate the presence of an Underground stone slab tomb.

== About the name ==
In the past, the name “Underground Taiseki Stone Chamber Tomb” (地下式板石積石室墓) was commonly used; however, because its origins lie in the construction of a “Sarcophagus” rather than a “stone chamber,” and since there is no corresponding “surface type” tomb with the same stone slab construction, the qualifier “underground” has lost its contrasting meaning. Consequently, in recent years the name “stone slab tomb” has come to be regarded as more appropriate.<ref name="Sfn|藤井|2009"/>

== Grave goods ==
Generally, few funerary goods are found in these tombs. Many contain no grave goods or only minimal iron weapons (such as swords and iron arrowheads), which has complicated the development of chronological frameworks and the establishment of a chronology for this tomb style. Among the iron weapons, iron arrowheads are most frequently recovered; these include forms such as the Keitō arrowhead, bird-beak arrowhead, and short-necked arrowhead.

== distribution ==
The distribution of stone slab tombs extends from the northern limit marked by the Ushimoku stone slab tomb Group in Ōaza Kamie, {{ill|Takanabe, Miyazaki|en|Takanabe, Miyazaki|WD=Q1206737|lt=Takanabe Town|1=Takanabe, Miyazaki}}, {{ill|Koyu District, Miyazaki|en|Koyu District, Miyazaki|WD=Q1132169|lt=Koyugu District|1=Koyu District, Miyazaki}}, {{ill|Miyazaki Prefecture|en|Miyazaki Prefecture|WD=Q130300|lt=Miyazaki Prefecture|1=Miyazaki Prefecture}}, to the southern limit represented by the Nakao stone slab tomb Group in {{ill|Aira, Kagoshima (Kimotsuki District)|en|Aira, Kagoshima (Kimotsuki District)|WD=Q4698402|lt=Awa-cho|1=Aira, Kagoshima (Kimotsuki District)}}, {{ill|Kanoya, Kagoshima|en|Kanoya, Kagoshima|WD=Q819578|lt=Kanoya City|1=Kanoya, Kagoshima}}, {{ill|Kagoshima Prefecture|en|Kagoshima Prefecture|WD=Q15701|lt=Kagoshima Prefecture|1=Kagoshima Prefecture}}. They are mainly distributed throughout the Miyazaki Plain, extending into basins in areas such as {{ill|Miyakonojō|en|Miyakonojō|WD=Q638301|lt=Tosu City|1=Miyakonojō}}, {{ill|Kobayashi, Miyazaki|en|Kobayashi, Miyazaki|WD=Q861283|lt=Kobayashi City|1=Kobayashi, Miyazaki}}, and {{ill|Ebino, Miyazaki|en|Ebino, Miyazaki|WD=Q374701|lt=Ebino City|1=Ebino, Miyazaki}} at the northern foothills of the {{ill|Kirishima Volcanic Group|ja|霧島火山群|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kirishima Volcanic Group|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 霧島山|1=Mount Kirishima|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q1319361}}, with the western boundary defined by the Harumura stone slab tomb Group in {{ill|Isa, Kagoshima|en|Isa, Kagoshima|WD=Q15736|lt=Isa City|1=Isa, Kagoshima}}, {{ill|Kagoshima Prefecture|en|Kagoshima Prefecture|WD=Q15701|lt=Kagoshima Prefecture|1=Kagoshima Prefecture}}. Additionally, two tombs have been identified at the Tendōgao site in {{ill|Hitoyoshi, Kumamoto|en|Hitoyoshi, Kumamoto|WD=Q861292|lt=Hitoyoshi City|1=Hitoyoshi, Kumamoto}}, {{ill|Kumamoto Prefecture|en|Kumamoto Prefecture|WD=Q130308|lt=Kumamoto Prefecture|1=Kumamoto Prefecture}}, indicating that the northwestern extent of this tomb style reaches into the basin of the {{ill|Kuma River (Japan)|en|Kuma River (Japan)|WD=Q1358183|lt=Kumagawa River|1=Kuma River (Japan)}}.

== Roots and development ==
The initial form of this tomb style is thought to be the “Yokuguchi-style Earthen Tomb” that appeared from the latter half of the early Kofun period to the early mid-Kofun period, discovered within a subgroup of the {{ill|Kogihara Underground Horizontal Yokoanabo Group|ja|小木原地下式横穴墓群|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kogihara Underground Horizontal Yokoanabo Group|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} in {{ill|Kobayashi, Miyazaki|en|Kobayashi, Miyazaki|WD=Q861283|lt=Kobayashi City|1=Kobayashi, Miyazaki}}, {{ill|Miyazaki Prefecture|en|Miyazaki Prefecture|WD=Q130300|lt=Miyazaki Prefecture|1=Miyazaki Prefecture}}. Subsequently, based on the shape of the burial chamber, these tombs were broadly categorized into two types—the “houseform type” and the “earthen mound type”—which spread regionally from the 5th to the 6th centuries.<ref name="Sfn|橋本|2012|p=143"/>

== Research History ==
Records of Underground Horizontal Yokoanabos date back to the {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period|1=Edo period}} and even earlier to the {{ill|Meiji period|ja|明治期|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Meiji period|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 明治|1=Meiji era|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q3125096}}. In the work ''{{ill|Keirin Manroku|ja|桂林漫録|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Keirin Manroku|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}'' by {{ill|Mori Island Nakayoshi|ja|森島（桂川）中良|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mori Island Nakayoshi|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, the younger brother of {{ill|Katsuragawa Hoshū|en|Katsuragawa Hoshū|WD=Q946932|lt=Katsuragawa Hoshu|1=Katsuragawa Hoshū}}, an account from 1789 (the 1st year of {{ill|Kansei|en|Kansei|WD=Q1195131|lt=Kansei|1=Kansei}}) describes a farmer in {{ill|Hyūga Province|en|Hyūga Province|WD=Q513737|lt=Hyūga Province|1=Hyūga Province}} near the pig mound at {{ill|Inoh-tsuka|ja|猪の塚|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Inoh-tsuka|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} (located in {{ill|Miyazaki Prefecture|en|Miyazaki Prefecture|WD=Q130300|lt=Miyazaki Prefecture|1=Miyazaki Prefecture}}, {{ill|Higashimorokata District, Miyazaki|en|Higashimorokata District, Miyazaki|WD=Q1132180|lt=Higashimorokata District|1=Higashimorokata District, Miyazaki}}, {{ill|Kunitomi, Miyazaki|en|Kunitomi, Miyazaki|WD=Q1350786|lt=Kunimoto Town|1=Kunitomi, Miyazaki}}, Honjō) who, while digging a trench, encountered a horizontal cave with its walls painted in vermilion, from which numerous relics were unearthed. Local historian {{ill|Senokuchi Denkurō|ja|瀬之口伝九郎|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Senokuchi Denkurō|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} regarded this as the earliest literary reference to an Underground Horizontal Yokoanabo.<ref name="Sfn|瀬之口|1919"/> In modern times, archaeological research began in earnest, and Senokuchi Denkurō coined the term “Underground-type Tomb” to classify it as one form of Kofun period burial system.<ref name="Sfn|瀬之口|1919"/>

Subsequently, studies employing archaeological methods—such as the classification of plan and cross-sectional morphologies, chronological analyses based on grave good assemblages, and examinations of the relationship between these tombs and keyhole-shaped tumuli—have steadily advanced.<ref name="Sfn|日高|1958"/><ref name="Sfn|石川|1973"/>

=== Discussion on "Hayato Burial System" ===
Parallel to these developments, a theory emerged proposing that Underground Horizontal Yokoanabos, owing to their unique structure, concentrated distribution in southern Kyushu, and the extremely sparse presence of keyhole-shaped tumuli in their principal distribution areas, were the tombs of the “Hayato,” a group regarded in ancient texts as peripheral by the centralized {{ill|Ritsuryō state|ja|律令国家|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ritsuryō state|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 律令制|1=Ritsuryō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q742460}}.<ref name="Sfn|高橋|1924"/> During the 1960s–80s, as comprehensive views of the Kofun period were synthesized, several scholars posited that stone slab tombs corresponded to the “Hayato tomb system” of the Hyūga–Ōsumi region, that Underground stone slab tombs in Satsuma corresponded to the “Satsuma Hayato tomb system,” and that certain tumuli-associated tombs in the southern Satsuma Peninsula represented the “Ata Hayato tomb system.”<ref name="Sfn|小田|1966|p=163"/><ref name="Sfn|乙益|1970"/><ref name="Sfn|上村|1984"/> Their formation was attributed to the region’s volcanic soils, limited flatlands unsuitable for rice cultivation, and its isolation from external influences, which led to a stagnation in cultural change from the Yayoi period onward and the establishment of an independent local sphere. This conceptualization—portraying the “specialized underground tomb system in southern Kyushu” as “Hayato tombs” in contrast to the expansive dominion of the {{ill|Yamato court|ja|大和朝廷|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yamato court|ja_comment=|2=ja|3=ヤマト王権|1=Yamato Kingship|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q2658252}}—gained widespread acceptance.

However, by the 1990s, many researchers, particularly local scholars in Kyushu, began to question the appropriateness of linking Underground Horizontal Yokoanabos with the “Hayato.”

The term “Hayato” first appears in the mythological portions of the {{ill|Kojiki|en|Kojiki|WD=Q813031|lt=Kojiki|1=Kojiki}}, and while it is mentioned from the time of Emperor Nintoku, its use as a confirmed historical term is generally recognized only from the 11th month of the 11th year of the {{ill|Tenmu period|ja|天武朝|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tenmu period|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} (682 AD, in records of Hayato tributary missions).<ref name="Sfn|中村|1993"/> Furthermore, the peak of Underground Horizontal Yokoanabo construction occurred during the 5th to 6th centuries, and there are no definitively dated examples persisting into the latter Kofun period (6th century). Similarly, Underground Horizontal Yokoanabos considered to be “Hayato tombs” in the Hyūga–Ōsumi region were primarily built in the 5th to 6th centuries, ceasing by the early 7th century. As for the so-called “Ata Hayato tombs” (represented by Tateishi Doikombō), the securely dated examples date from the mid-Yayoi to the early Kofun period, and in that region (from the southern tip of the Satsuma Peninsula to the coastal areas of Kagoshima Bay), tomb types without tumuli or with pottery coffins are predominant, making it less tenable to designate that tomb system solely as “Ata Hayato tombs.” Moreover, some scholars argue that the very concept of “Hayato” was a pseudo-ethnic construct, politically created by the Ritsuryō government based on Sinocentric ideology, rather than arising from indigenous ethnic differences.<ref name="Sfn|永山|2009|pp=40"/><ref name="Sfn|中村|1993"/><ref name="Sfn|東|2001|p=498"/><ref name="Sfn|原口|2008"/><ref name="Sfn|原口|2011"/>

=== Research after the theory of "Hayato Burial System" ===
From the 2000s onward, research on stone slab tombs has increasingly employed extensive excavation data and artifact assemblages to examine these tombs using rigorous archaeological methods, conceptualizing them as a regional burial system of the Kofun period. Detailed studies now focus on classification based on structural morphology, chronological frameworks derived from grave good composition and distribution patterns, and reconstructions of social hierarchy and regional structure based on the relationship with keyhole-shaped tumuli.<ref name="Sfn|第6回九州前方後円墳研究会|2003"/><ref name="Sfn|橋本|2009c"/><ref name="Sfn|藤井|2009"/>

[[File:板石積石棺墓（地下式板石積石室墓）.png|350px|thumb|{{ill|Schematic diagram of an Underground stone slab tomb|ja|板石積石棺墓（地下式板石積石室墓）|lt=Schematic diagram of an Underground stone slab tomb|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Schematic diagram of an Underground stone slab tomb|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}]]
'''stone slab tomb''' (板石積石棺墓), also known as '''Underground stone slab tomb''' (地下式板石積石室墓), is a type of Sarcophagus tomb in which a circular or square burial pit is excavated in the ground and flat stone slabs are arranged vertically along the walls, being successively overlapped in a “carrying” manner to form a lid. It is recognized as a regionally distinctive tomb style that emerged during the 4th–5th centuries of the {{ill|Kofun period|en|Kofun period|WD=Q459939|lt=Kofun period|1=Kofun period}} in the southern part of the {{ill|Kyushu region|ja|九州地方|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kyushu region|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 九州|1=Kyushu|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q13987}}, particularly from the northwestern part of {{ill|Kagoshima Prefecture|en|Kagoshima Prefecture|WD=Q15701|lt=Kagoshima Prefecture|1=Kagoshima Prefecture}}, extending to the island areas along the western coast of Kyushu and the southwestern part of {{ill|Miyazaki Prefecture|en|Miyazaki Prefecture|WD=Q130300|lt=Miyazaki Prefecture|1=Miyazaki Prefecture}}.

==Overview==

=== structure ===
A burial pit of either circular or square plan is excavated in the ground. Along its walls, stone slabs (known as side stones) are set upright so as to form a Sarcophagus (the burial facility). Flat stone slabs are then laid on top of the side stones and further slabs are gradually overlapped with slight offsets—a method known as “carrying”—to build up the height and form a domed ceiling lid. Finally, the pit is backfilled with earth, thus creating an underground burial space. When the overlying soil is removed during excavation surveys, especially in cases with a circular plan, the dome structure formed by the overlapping slabs often exhibits a characteristic “fish-scale” or “chrysanthemum” appearance. Variations exist in plan shape, with some tombs being circular and others square or rectangular, and several classification schemes have been proposed. Debates continue regarding which form predates the other, as well as the origins and genealogical development of this tomb style.

=== Group Structure ===
It is extremely rare for a single stone slab tomb to be constructed in isolation; instead, they are typically found clustered in groups of two to three or even in dense groups of more than a dozen. Accordingly, the archaeological site is usually designated as “(Place Name) + stone slab tomb Group.” However, because they often occur alongside tombs from other periods—such as earthen mound tombs or Underground Horizontal Yokoanabos—some sites are simply referred to as “(Place Name) + Site.”

=== Above-ground structures ===
In most cases, there are no surface structures or markers resembling the tumuli of keyhole-shaped Kofuns. Consequently, the locations of these tombs were often not recognized by later generations. There are instances where a sudden collapse of the burial chamber ceiling caused the ground surface to subside, leading to the tomb’s discovery, or where agricultural activities (such as plowing or land improvement) resulted in farm animals or tractors becoming caught in a collapsed chamber, effectively uncovering the tomb accidentally.<ref name="Sfn|藤井|2009"/> In recent years, buried cultural property surveys have sometimes employed ground-penetrating radar to identify the tomb locations. Furthermore, the Board of Education of Miyazaki City has issued warnings on its website regarding sudden ground subsidence in agricultural fields, noting that such events may indicate the presence of an Underground stone slab tomb.

== About the name ==
In the past, the name “Underground Taiseki Stone Chamber Tomb” (地下式板石積石室墓) was commonly used; however, because its origins lie in the construction of a “Sarcophagus” rather than a “stone chamber,” and since there is no corresponding “surface type” tomb with the same stone slab construction, the qualifier “underground” has lost its contrasting meaning. Consequently, in recent years the name “stone slab tomb” has come to be regarded as more appropriate.<ref name="Sfn|藤井|2009"/>

== Grave goods ==
Generally, few funerary goods are found in these tombs. Many contain no grave goods or only minimal iron weapons (such as swords and iron arrowheads), which has complicated the development of chronological frameworks and the establishment of a chronology for this tomb style. Among the iron weapons, iron arrowheads are most frequently recovered; these include forms such as the Keitō arrowhead, bird-beak arrowhead, and short-necked arrowhead.

== distribution ==
The distribution of stone slab tombs extends from the northern limit marked by the Ushimoku stone slab tomb Group in Ōaza Kamie, {{ill|Takanabe, Miyazaki|en|Takanabe, Miyazaki|WD=Q1206737|lt=Takanabe Town|1=Takanabe, Miyazaki}}, {{ill|Koyu District, Miyazaki|en|Koyu District, Miyazaki|WD=Q1132169|lt=Koyugu District|1=Koyu District, Miyazaki}}, {{ill|Miyazaki Prefecture|en|Miyazaki Prefecture|WD=Q130300|lt=Miyazaki Prefecture|1=Miyazaki Prefecture}}, to the southern limit represented by the Nakao stone slab tomb Group in {{ill|Aira, Kagoshima (Kimotsuki District)|en|Aira, Kagoshima (Kimotsuki District)|WD=Q4698402|lt=Awa-cho|1=Aira, Kagoshima (Kimotsuki District)}}, {{ill|Kanoya, Kagoshima|en|Kanoya, Kagoshima|WD=Q819578|lt=Kanoya City|1=Kanoya, Kagoshima}}, {{ill|Kagoshima Prefecture|en|Kagoshima Prefecture|WD=Q15701|lt=Kagoshima Prefecture|1=Kagoshima Prefecture}}. They are mainly distributed throughout the Miyazaki Plain, extending into basins in areas such as {{ill|Miyakonojō|en|Miyakonojō|WD=Q638301|lt=Tosu City|1=Miyakonojō}}, {{ill|Kobayashi, Miyazaki|en|Kobayashi, Miyazaki|WD=Q861283|lt=Kobayashi City|1=Kobayashi, Miyazaki}}, and {{ill|Ebino, Miyazaki|en|Ebino, Miyazaki|WD=Q374701|lt=Ebino City|1=Ebino, Miyazaki}} at the northern foothills of the {{ill|Kirishima Volcanic Group|ja|霧島火山群|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kirishima Volcanic Group|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 霧島山|1=Mount Kirishima|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q1319361}}, with the western boundary defined by the Harumura stone slab tomb Group in {{ill|Isa, Kagoshima|en|Isa, Kagoshima|WD=Q15736|lt=Isa City|1=Isa, Kagoshima}}, {{ill|Kagoshima Prefecture|en|Kagoshima Prefecture|WD=Q15701|lt=Kagoshima Prefecture|1=Kagoshima Prefecture}}. Additionally, two tombs have been identified at the Tendōgao site in {{ill|Hitoyoshi, Kumamoto|en|Hitoyoshi, Kumamoto|WD=Q861292|lt=Hitoyoshi City|1=Hitoyoshi, Kumamoto}}, {{ill|Kumamoto Prefecture|en|Kumamoto Prefecture|WD=Q130308|lt=Kumamoto Prefecture|1=Kumamoto Prefecture}}, indicating that the northwestern extent of this tomb style reaches into the basin of the {{ill|Kuma River (Japan)|en|Kuma River (Japan)|WD=Q1358183|lt=Kumagawa River|1=Kuma River (Japan)}}.

== Roots and development ==
The initial form of this tomb style is thought to be the “Yokuguchi-style Earthen Tomb” that appeared from the latter half of the early Kofun period to the early mid-Kofun period, discovered within a subgroup of the {{ill|Kogihara Underground Horizontal Yokoanabo Group|ja|小木原地下式横穴墓群|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kogihara Underground Horizontal Yokoanabo Group|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} in {{ill|Kobayashi, Miyazaki|en|Kobayashi, Miyazaki|WD=Q861283|lt=Kobayashi City|1=Kobayashi, Miyazaki}}, {{ill|Miyazaki Prefecture|en|Miyazaki Prefecture|WD=Q130300|lt=Miyazaki Prefecture|1=Miyazaki Prefecture}}. Subsequently, based on the shape of the burial chamber, these tombs were broadly categorized into two types—the “houseform type” and the “earthen mound type”—which spread regionally from the 5th to the 6th centuries.<ref name="Sfn|橋本|2012|p=143"/>

== Research History ==
Records of Underground Horizontal Yokoanabos date back to the {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period|1=Edo period}} and even earlier to the {{ill|Meiji period|ja|明治期|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Meiji period|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 明治|1=Meiji era|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q3125096}}. In the work ''{{ill|Keirin Manroku|ja|桂林漫録|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Keirin Manroku|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}'' by {{ill|Mori Island Nakayoshi|ja|森島（桂川）中良|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mori Island Nakayoshi|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, the younger brother of {{ill|Katsuragawa Hoshū|en|Katsuragawa Hoshū|WD=Q946932|lt=Katsuragawa Hoshu|1=Katsuragawa Hoshū}}, an account from 1789 (the 1st year of {{ill|Kansei|en|Kansei|WD=Q1195131|lt=Kansei|1=Kansei}}) describes a farmer in {{ill|Hyūga Province|en|Hyūga Province|WD=Q513737|lt=Hyūga Province|1=Hyūga Province}} near the pig mound at {{ill|Inoh-tsuka|ja|猪の塚|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Inoh-tsuka|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} (located in {{ill|Miyazaki Prefecture|en|Miyazaki Prefecture|WD=Q130300|lt=Miyazaki Prefecture|1=Miyazaki Prefecture}}, {{ill|Higashimorokata District, Miyazaki|en|Higashimorokata District, Miyazaki|WD=Q1132180|lt=Higashimorokata District|1=Higashimorokata District, Miyazaki}}, {{ill|Kunitomi, Miyazaki|en|Kunitomi, Miyazaki|WD=Q1350786|lt=Kunimoto Town|1=Kunitomi, Miyazaki}}, Honjō) who, while digging a trench, encountered a horizontal cave with its walls painted in vermilion, from which numerous relics were unearthed. Local historian {{ill|Senokuchi Denkurō|ja|瀬之口伝九郎|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Senokuchi Denkurō|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} regarded this as the earliest literary reference to an Underground Horizontal Yokoanabo.<ref name="Sfn|瀬之口|1919"/> In modern times, archaeological research began in earnest, and Senokuchi Denkurō coined the term “Underground-type Tomb” to classify it as one form of Kofun period burial system.<ref name="Sfn|瀬之口|1919"/>

Subsequently, studies employing archaeological methods—such as the classification of plan and cross-sectional morphologies, chronological analyses based on grave good assemblages, and examinations of the relationship between these tombs and keyhole-shaped tumuli—have steadily advanced.<ref name="Sfn|日高|1958"/><ref name="Sfn|石川|1973"/>

=== Discussion on "Hayato Burial System" ===
Parallel to these developments, a theory emerged proposing that Underground Horizontal Yokoanabos, owing to their unique structure, concentrated distribution in southern Kyushu, and the extremely sparse presence of keyhole-shaped tumuli in their principal distribution areas, were the tombs of the “Hayato,” a group regarded in ancient texts as peripheral by the centralized {{ill|Ritsuryō state|ja|律令国家|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ritsuryō state|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 律令制|1=Ritsuryō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q742460}}.<ref name="Sfn|高橋|1924"/> During the 1960s–80s, as comprehensive views of the Kofun period were synthesized, several scholars posited that stone slab tombs corresponded to the “Hayato tomb system” of the Hyūga–Ōsumi region, that Underground stone slab tombs in Satsuma corresponded to the “Satsuma Hayato tomb system,” and that certain tumuli-associated tombs in the southern Satsuma Peninsula represented the “Ata Hayato tomb system.”<ref name="Sfn|小田|1966|p=163"/><ref name="Sfn|乙益|1970"/><ref name="Sfn|上村|1984"/> Their formation was attributed to the region’s volcanic soils, limited flatlands unsuitable for rice cultivation, and its isolation from external influences, which led to a stagnation in cultural change from the Yayoi period onward and the establishment of an independent local sphere. This conceptualization—portraying the “specialized underground tomb system in southern Kyushu” as “Hayato tombs” in contrast to the expansive dominion of the {{ill|Yamato court|ja|大和朝廷|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yamato court|ja_comment=|2=ja|3=ヤマト王権|1=Yamato Kingship|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q2658252}}—gained widespread acceptance.

However, by the 1990s, many researchers, particularly local scholars in Kyushu, began to question the appropriateness of linking Underground Horizontal Yokoanabos with the “Hayato.”

The term “Hayato” first appears in the mythological portions of the {{ill|Kojiki|en|Kojiki|WD=Q813031|lt=Kojiki|1=Kojiki}}, and while it is mentioned from the time of Emperor Nintoku, its use as a confirmed historical term is generally recognized only from the 11th month of the 11th year of the {{ill|Tenmu period|ja|天武朝|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tenmu period|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} (682 AD, in records of Hayato tributary missions).<ref name="Sfn|中村|1993"/> Furthermore, the peak of Underground Horizontal Yokoanabo construction occurred during the 5th to 6th centuries, and there are no definitively dated examples persisting into the latter Kofun period (6th century). Similarly, Underground Horizontal Yokoanabos considered to be “Hayato tombs” in the Hyūga–Ōsumi region were primarily built in the 5th to 6th centuries, ceasing by the early 7th century. As for the so-called “Ata Hayato tombs” (represented by Tateishi Doikombō), the securely dated examples date from the mid-Yayoi to the early Kofun period, and in that region (from the southern tip of the Satsuma Peninsula to the coastal areas of Kagoshima Bay), tomb types without tumuli or with pottery coffins are predominant, making it less tenable to designate that tomb system solely as “Ata Hayato tombs.” Moreover, some scholars argue that the very concept of “Hayato” was a pseudo-ethnic construct, politically created by the Ritsuryō government based on Sinocentric ideology, rather than arising from indigenous ethnic differences.<ref name="Sfn|永山|2009|pp=40"/><ref name="Sfn|中村|1993"/><ref name="Sfn|東|2001|p=498"/><ref name="Sfn|原口|2008"/><ref name="Sfn|原口|2011"/>

=== Research after the theory of "Hayato Burial System" ===
From the 2000s onward, research on stone slab tombs has increasingly employed extensive excavation data and artifact assemblages to examine these tombs using rigorous archaeological methods, conceptualizing them as a regional burial system of the Kofun period. Detailed studies now focus on classification based on structural morphology, chronological frameworks derived from grave good composition and distribution patterns, and reconstructions of social hierarchy and regional structure based on the relationship with keyhole-shaped tumuli.<ref name="Sfn|第6回九州前方後円墳研究会|2003"/><ref name="Sfn|橋本|2009c"/><ref name="Sfn|藤井|2009"/>

[[File:板石積石棺墓（地下式板石積石室墓）.png|350px|thumb|{{ill|Schematic diagram of an Underground stone slab tomb|ja|板石積石棺墓（地下式板石積石室墓）|lt=Schematic diagram of an Underground stone slab tomb|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Schematic diagram of an Underground stone slab tomb|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}]]
'''stone slab tomb''' (板石積石棺墓), also known as '''Underground stone slab tomb''' (地下式板石積石室墓), is a type of Sarcophagus tomb in which a circular or square burial pit is excavated in the ground and flat stone slabs are arranged vertically along the walls, being successively overlapped in a “carrying” manner to form a lid. It is recognized as a regionally distinctive tomb style that emerged during the 4th–5th centuries of the {{ill|Kofun period|en|Kofun period|WD=Q459939|lt=Kofun period|1=Kofun period}} in the southern part of the {{ill|Kyushu region|ja|九州地方|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kyushu region|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 九州|1=Kyushu|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q13987}}, particularly from the northwestern part of {{ill|Kagoshima Prefecture|en|Kagoshima Prefecture|WD=Q15701|lt=Kagoshima Prefecture|1=Kagoshima Prefecture}}, extending to the island areas along the western coast of Kyushu and the southwestern part of {{ill|Miyazaki Prefecture|en|Miyazaki Prefecture|WD=Q130300|lt=Miyazaki Prefecture|1=Miyazaki Prefecture}}.

==Overview==

=== structure ===
A burial pit of either circular or square plan is excavated in the ground. Along its walls, stone slabs (known as side stones) are set upright so as to form a Sarcophagus (the burial facility). Flat stone slabs are then laid on top of the side stones and further slabs are gradually overlapped with slight offsets—a method known as “carrying”—to build up the height and form a domed ceiling lid. Finally, the pit is backfilled with earth, thus creating an underground burial space. When the overlying soil is removed during excavation surveys, especially in cases with a circular plan, the dome structure formed by the overlapping slabs often exhibits a characteristic “fish-scale” or “chrysanthemum” appearance. Variations exist in plan shape, with some tombs being circular and others square or rectangular, and several classification schemes have been proposed. Debates continue regarding which form predates the other, as well as the origins and genealogical development of this tomb style.

=== Group Structure ===
It is extremely rare for a single stone slab tomb to be constructed in isolation; instead, they are typically found clustered in groups of two to three or even in dense groups of more than a dozen. Accordingly, the archaeological site is usually designated as “(Place Name) + stone slab tomb Group.” However, because they often occur alongside tombs from other periods—such as earthen mound tombs or Underground Horizontal Yokoanabos—some sites are simply referred to as “(Place Name) + Site.”

=== Above-ground structures ===
In most cases, there are no surface structures or markers resembling the tumuli of keyhole-shaped Kofuns. Consequently, the locations of these tombs were often not recognized by later generations. There are instances where a sudden collapse of the burial chamber ceiling caused the ground surface to subside, leading to the tomb’s discovery, or where agricultural activities (such as plowing or land improvement) resulted in farm animals or tractors becoming caught in a collapsed chamber, effectively uncovering the tomb accidentally.<ref name="Sfn|藤井|2009"/> In recent years, buried cultural property surveys have sometimes employed ground-penetrating radar to identify the tomb locations. Furthermore, the Board of Education of Miyazaki City has issued warnings on its website regarding sudden ground subsidence in agricultural fields, noting that such events may indicate the presence of an Underground stone slab tomb.

== About the name ==
In the past, the name “Underground Taiseki Stone Chamber Tomb” (地下式板石積石室墓) was commonly used; however, because its origins lie in the construction of a “Sarcophagus” rather than a “stone chamber,” and since there is no corresponding “surface type” tomb with the same stone slab construction, the qualifier “underground” has lost its contrasting meaning. Consequently, in recent years the name “stone slab tomb” has come to be regarded as more appropriate.<ref name="Sfn|藤井|2009"/>

== Grave goods ==
Generally, few funerary goods are found in these tombs. Many contain no grave goods or only minimal iron weapons (such as swords and iron arrowheads), which has complicated the development of chronological frameworks and the establishment of a chronology for this tomb style. Among the iron weapons, iron arrowheads are most frequently recovered; these include forms such as the Keitō arrowhead, bird-beak arrowhead, and short-necked arrowhead.

== distribution ==
The distribution of stone slab tombs extends from the northern limit marked by the Ushimoku stone slab tomb Group in Ōaza Kamie, {{ill|Takanabe, Miyazaki|en|Takanabe, Miyazaki|WD=Q1206737|lt=Takanabe Town|1=Takanabe, Miyazaki}}, {{ill|Koyu District, Miyazaki|en|Koyu District, Miyazaki|WD=Q1132169|lt=Koyugu District|1=Koyu District, Miyazaki}}, {{ill|Miyazaki Prefecture|en|Miyazaki Prefecture|WD=Q130300|lt=Miyazaki Prefecture|1=Miyazaki Prefecture}}, to the southern limit represented by the Nakao stone slab tomb Group in {{ill|Aira, Kagoshima (Kimotsuki District)|en|Aira, Kagoshima (Kimotsuki District)|WD=Q4698402|lt=Awa-cho|1=Aira, Kagoshima (Kimotsuki District)}}, {{ill|Kanoya, Kagoshima|en|Kanoya, Kagoshima|WD=Q819578|lt=Kanoya City|1=Kanoya, Kagoshima}}, {{ill|Kagoshima Prefecture|en|Kagoshima Prefecture|WD=Q15701|lt=Kagoshima Prefecture|1=Kagoshima Prefecture}}. They are mainly distributed throughout the Miyazaki Plain, extending into basins in areas such as {{ill|Miyakonojō|en|Miyakonojō|WD=Q638301|lt=Tosu City|1=Miyakonojō}}, {{ill|Kobayashi, Miyazaki|en|Kobayashi, Miyazaki|WD=Q861283|lt=Kobayashi City|1=Kobayashi, Miyazaki}}, and {{ill|Ebino, Miyazaki|en|Ebino, Miyazaki|WD=Q374701|lt=Ebino City|1=Ebino, Miyazaki}} at the northern foothills of the {{ill|Kirishima Volcanic Group|ja|霧島火山群|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kirishima Volcanic Group|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 霧島山|1=Mount Kirishima|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q1319361}}, with the western boundary defined by the Harumura stone slab tomb Group in {{ill|Isa, Kagoshima|en|Isa, Kagoshima|WD=Q15736|lt=Isa City|1=Isa, Kagoshima}}, {{ill|Kagoshima Prefecture|en|Kagoshima Prefecture|WD=Q15701|lt=Kagoshima Prefecture|1=Kagoshima Prefecture}}. Additionally, two tombs have been identified at the Tendōgao site in {{ill|Hitoyoshi, Kumamoto|en|Hitoyoshi, Kumamoto|WD=Q861292|lt=Hitoyoshi City|1=Hitoyoshi, Kumamoto}}, {{ill|Kumamoto Prefecture|en|Kumamoto Prefecture|WD=Q130308|lt=Kumamoto Prefecture|1=Kumamoto Prefecture}}, indicating that the northwestern extent of this tomb style reaches into the basin of the {{ill|Kuma River (Japan)|en|Kuma River (Japan)|WD=Q1358183|lt=Kumagawa River|1=Kuma River (Japan)}}.

== Roots and development ==
The initial form of this tomb style is thought to be the “Yokuguchi-style Earthen Tomb” that appeared from the latter half of the early Kofun period to the early mid-Kofun period, discovered within a subgroup of the {{ill|Kogihara Underground Horizontal Yokoanabo Group|ja|小木原地下式横穴墓群|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kogihara Underground Horizontal Yokoanabo Group|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} in {{ill|Kobayashi, Miyazaki|en|Kobayashi, Miyazaki|WD=Q861283|lt=Kobayashi City|1=Kobayashi, Miyazaki}}, {{ill|Miyazaki Prefecture|en|Miyazaki Prefecture|WD=Q130300|lt=Miyazaki Prefecture|1=Miyazaki Prefecture}}. Subsequently, based on the shape of the burial chamber, these tombs were broadly categorized into two types—the “houseform type” and the “earthen mound type”—which spread regionally from the 5th to the 6th centuries.<ref name="Sfn|橋本|2012|p=143"/>

== Research History ==
Records of Underground Horizontal Yokoanabos date back to the {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period|1=Edo period}} and even earlier to the {{ill|Meiji period|ja|明治期|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Meiji period|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 明治|1=Meiji era|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q3125096}}. In the work ''{{ill|Keirin Manroku|ja|桂林漫録|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Keirin Manroku|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}'' by {{ill|Mori Island Nakayoshi|ja|森島（桂川）中良|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mori Island Nakayoshi|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, the younger brother of {{ill|Katsuragawa Hoshū|en|Katsuragawa Hoshū|WD=Q946932|lt=Katsuragawa Hoshu|1=Katsuragawa Hoshū}}, an account from 1789 (the 1st year of {{ill|Kansei|en|Kansei|WD=Q1195131|lt=Kansei|1=Kansei}}) describes a farmer in {{ill|Hyūga Province|en|Hyūga Province|WD=Q513737|lt=Hyūga Province|1=Hyūga Province}} near the pig mound at {{ill|Inoh-tsuka|ja|猪の塚|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Inoh-tsuka|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} (located in {{ill|Miyazaki Prefecture|en|Miyazaki Prefecture|WD=Q130300|lt=Miyazaki Prefecture|1=Miyazaki Prefecture}}, {{ill|Higashimorokata District, Miyazaki|en|Higashimorokata District, Miyazaki|WD=Q1132180|lt=Higashimorokata District|1=Higashimorokata District, Miyazaki}}, {{ill|Kunitomi, Miyazaki|en|Kunitomi, Miyazaki|WD=Q1350786|lt=Kunimoto Town|1=Kunitomi, Miyazaki}}, Honjō) who, while digging a trench, encountered a horizontal cave with its walls painted in vermilion, from which numerous relics were unearthed. Local historian {{ill|Senokuchi Denkurō|ja|瀬之口伝九郎|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Senokuchi Denkurō|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} regarded this as the earliest literary reference to an Underground Horizontal Yokoanabo.<ref name="Sfn|瀬之口|1919"/> In modern times, archaeological research began in earnest, and Senokuchi Denkurō coined the term “Underground-type Tomb” to classify it as one form of Kofun period burial system.<ref name="Sfn|瀬之口|1919"/>

Subsequently, studies employing archaeological methods—such as the classification of plan and cross-sectional morphologies, chronological analyses based on grave good assemblages, and examinations of the relationship between these tombs and keyhole-shaped tumuli—have steadily advanced.<ref name="Sfn|日高|1958"/><ref name="Sfn|石川|1973"/>

=== Discussion on "Hayato Burial System" ===
Parallel to these developments, a theory emerged proposing that Underground Horizontal Yokoanabos, owing to their unique structure, concentrated distribution in southern Kyushu, and the extremely sparse presence of keyhole-shaped tumuli in their principal distribution areas, were the tombs of the “Hayato,” a group regarded in ancient texts as peripheral by the centralized {{ill|Ritsuryō state|ja|律令国家|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ritsuryō state|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 律令制|1=Ritsuryō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q742460}}.<ref name="Sfn|高橋|1924"/> During the 1960s–80s, as comprehensive views of the Kofun period were synthesized, several scholars posited that stone slab tombs corresponded to the “Hayato tomb system” of the Hyūga–Ōsumi region, that Underground stone slab tombs in Satsuma corresponded to the “Satsuma Hayato tomb system,” and that certain tumuli-associated tombs in the southern Satsuma Peninsula represented the “Ata Hayato tomb system.”<ref name="Sfn|小田|1966|p=163"/><ref name="Sfn|乙益|1970"/><ref name="Sfn|上村|1984"/> Their formation was attributed to the region’s volcanic soils, limited flatlands unsuitable for rice cultivation, and its isolation from external influences, which led to a stagnation in cultural change from the Yayoi period onward and the establishment of an independent local sphere. This conceptualization—portraying the “specialized underground tomb system in southern Kyushu” as “Hayato tombs” in contrast to the expansive dominion of the {{ill|Yamato court|ja|大和朝廷|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yamato court|ja_comment=|2=ja|3=ヤマト王権|1=Yamato Kingship|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q2658252}}—gained widespread acceptance.

However, by the 1990s, many researchers, particularly local scholars in Kyushu, began to question the appropriateness of linking Underground Horizontal Yokoanabos with the “Hayato.”

The term “Hayato” first appears in the mythological portions of the {{ill|Kojiki|en|Kojiki|WD=Q813031|lt=Kojiki|1=Kojiki}}, and while it is mentioned from the time of Emperor Nintoku, its use as a confirmed historical term is generally recognized only from the 11th month of the 11th year of the {{ill|Tenmu period|ja|天武朝|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tenmu period|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} (682 AD, in records of Hayato tributary missions).<ref name="Sfn|中村|1993"/> Furthermore, the peak of Underground Horizontal Yokoanabo construction occurred during the 5th to 6th centuries, and there are no definitively dated examples persisting into the latter Kofun period (6th century). Similarly, Underground Horizontal Yokoanabos considered to be “Hayato tombs” in the Hyūga–Ōsumi region were primarily built in the 5th to 6th centuries, ceasing by the early 7th century. As for the so-called “Ata Hayato tombs” (represented by Tateishi Doikombō), the securely dated examples date from the mid-Yayoi to the early Kofun period, and in that region (from the southern tip of the Satsuma Peninsula to the coastal areas of Kagoshima Bay), tomb types without tumuli or with pottery coffins are predominant, making it less tenable to designate that tomb system solely as “Ata Hayato tombs.” Moreover, some scholars argue that the very concept of “Hayato” was a pseudo-ethnic construct, politically created by the Ritsuryō government based on Sinocentric ideology, rather than arising from indigenous ethnic differences.<ref name="Sfn|永山|2009|pp=40"/><ref name="Sfn|中村|1993"/><ref name="Sfn|東|2001|p=498"/><ref name="Sfn|原口|2008"/><ref name="Sfn|原口|2011"/>

=== Research after the theory of "Hayato Burial System" ===
From the 2000s onward, research on stone slab tombs has increasingly employed extensive excavation data and artifact assemblages to examine these tombs using rigorous archaeological methods, conceptualizing them as a regional burial system of the Kofun period. Detailed studies now focus on classification based on structural morphology, chronological frameworks derived from grave good composition and distribution patterns, and reconstructions of social hierarchy and regional structure based on the relationship with keyhole-shaped tumuli.<ref name="Sfn|第6回九州前方後円墳研究会|2003"/><ref name="Sfn|橋本|2009c"/><ref name="Sfn|藤井|2009"/>

<!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[ja:板石積石棺墓]]
